street_smart.title: You're in a packed Bengaluru Metro queue during rush hour when the person behind you keeps shoving forward — words are exchanged, and it turns physical, just like today's queue dispute where a commuter punched another. What do you do in the moment?
street_smart.based_on: Today's real Bengaluru news: a Metro queue dispute turned violent when one commuter punched another (The Times of India).
street_smart.situation: You're near the front of a long security queue at a Metro station. Someone behind you pushes past, you ask them to wait their turn, and the exchange escalates — they shove you and look ready to swing.

choices.text: Step back to create distance, raise your voice to draw attention, and get the nearest CISF/BMRCL security staff or the platform's emergency intercom involved.
choices.feedback: Correct. Every Namma Metro station has security staff on duty specifically for this — creating distance first and letting them intervene keeps you out of physical danger and out of a legal mess.

choices.text: Push back or throw a punch yourself since they hit first — you're just standing your ground.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Under Indian law, police can and do book both parties in a mutual scuffle regardless of who struck first, and CCTV rarely proves who "started" it — retaliating turns you from a victim into a co-accused.

choices.text: Pull out your phone to film the confrontation up close instead of calling for help, planning to post it online later.
choices.feedback: Risky. Filming from within arm's reach doesn't create distance from someone who's already escalating, and a video posted later does nothing for your safety right now — get help first, film from a safe distance if at all.

choices.text: Say nothing and quietly let them cut ahead, hoping that ends it.
choices.feedback: Risky. Conceding can work, but someone already aggressive enough to shove you isn't guaranteed to stop there — moving to a safer position and flagging staff is a more reliable exit than just hoping it de-escalates.

takeaways: Every Namma Metro station has CISF/BMRCL security on duty — in a queue altercation, create distance and flag them rather than engaging.
Indian law can book both sides of a mutual physical scuffle, so hitting back — even in response to being hit first — carries real legal risk of its own.
If you record an altercation, do it from a safe distance after you've already sought help, not up close instead of it.

quiz.question: Bengaluru's new draft on-street parking rules would charge how much per year for parking outside your home, at the top end?
quiz.why: The hourly rate is proposed at Rs 10-80/hour, and the rules are meant to push vehicle owners toward off-street parking.

quiz.question: Which August 15 Bengaluru event has drawn 18,000+ registrations and comes with traffic curbs and a Metro station closure?
quiz.why: It's being held at Vidhana Soudha with a parade, art installations and building tours, using QR-code entry for registered visitors.

quiz.question: The RBI announced it will prematurely end which facility, with deposits accepted only till August 31?
quiz.why: FCNR(B) accounts let NRIs hold foreign-currency deposits in Indian banks; the swap facility was a temporary RBI tool to attract such inflows.

quiz.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution lets citizens move the Supreme Court directly to enforce their fundamental rights?
quiz.why: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the "heart and soul" of the Constitution — a fitting fact just ahead of Independence Day.

quiz.question: Which wind system brings the bulk of Karnataka's rainfall, including Bengaluru's, between June and September?
quiz.why: The Northeast Monsoon (Oct-Dec) matters more for Tamil Nadu's coast; Karnataka's interior gets most of its rain from the Southwest Monsoon, which is why today's heavy drizzle fits the seasonal pattern.
